subject: English
name: English, Units 3 and 4
about: VCE, Text response, creating texts and argument analysis
syllabus: VCE English and EAL Study Design (from 2023), Units 3 and 4

points.title: The analytical text response
points.brief: An essay that answers a topic about a set text with a clear contention, organised paragraphs and close use of evidence.

points.title: Reading an essay topic
points.brief: Breaking a topic into its terms, its assumption and its instruction word shows what the essay must argue.

points.title: Kinds of essay topics
points.brief: Topics may ask about a theme, a character, a quotation or how the text is constructed, and each needs a different focus.

points.title: The dynamics of a text
points.brief: Characters' motives, tensions in relationships, what settings do, twists in the plot and point of view all work together in a text.

points.title: Forming an interpretation
points.brief: An interpretation is your reading of what the text suggests, backed by evidence, which can differ from other readings.

points.title: Views and values of the author
points.brief: A text shows its historical context and social and cultural values, and the writer's choices hint at what they support or criticise.

points.title: How form shapes meaning
points.brief: A novel, play, film, poetry collection or memoir each make meaning in their own ways, such as stage directions or camera angles.

points.title: Using metalanguage
points.brief: Terms such as motif, juxtaposition and characterisation let a writer name exactly how a text makes meaning.

points.title: Writing an introduction
points.brief: An introduction names the text and writer, responds to the topic with a contention, and maps the main points.

points.title: Writing a conclusion
points.brief: A conclusion draws the argument together and returns to the topic, without simply repeating the paragraphs.

points.title: Frameworks of ideas
points.brief: Creating texts is built around one framework of ideas, such as writing about country, protest, personal journeys or play.

points.title: Reading mentor texts closely
points.brief: Mentor texts show techniques to borrow, such as an opening image, a shift in tense or a repeated line.

points.title: Writing about country
points.brief: A framework exploring place and belonging, and the bonds between people and the places they know.

points.title: Writing about protest
points.brief: A framework exploring why people speak out, resist or refuse, and the forms protest takes.

points.title: Writing about personal journeys
points.brief: A framework exploring change, growth, identity and the paths people travel, literally or not.

points.title: Writing about play
points.brief: A framework exploring games, imagination, sport and fun, and what play shows about people.

points.title: Choosing a form for a purpose
points.brief: Writers pick a form, such as a personal essay, short story, speech or opinion piece, that best suits their idea and audience.

points.title: Writing with a clear purpose
points.brief: Every piece aims to express, reflect, explain or argue, and its language is honed to serve that aim.

points.title: Language modes in Unit 3
points.brief: A piece written to be read, heard or watched is shaped by its mode, which changes its structure and how it makes meaning.

points.title: Standard and non-standard language
points.brief: Writers can choose slang, dialect or broken rules on purpose, when it suits the voice, audience and context.

points.title: The commentary on your writing
points.brief: A short commentary on the choices in your own piece: purpose, audience, context and language, and how the mentor texts shaped them.

units.title: Unit 4: Reading texts and analysing argument

chapters.title: Reading and responding to a second text

points.title: Comparing ideas across a text
points.brief: Strong essays trace how an idea develops, shifts or contrasts across the whole text, not just in one scene.

points.title: Structure in an essay
points.brief: Paragraphs can each take one argument, building from a simpler point to a deeper one.

points.title: Embedding evidence
points.brief: Short quotations built into your own sentences, followed by analysis of their language, show close reading.

points.title: Discussing different readings
points.brief: Acknowledging that a moment can be read in more than one way, then arguing for one, shows depth.

points.title: Identifying the contention and tone
points.brief: Analysis starts with what the writer argues, to whom, in what tone and in what context.

points.title: Analysing language for persuasive effect
points.brief: Good analysis names a technique and explains how it is meant to position the reader, using the writer's words.

points.title: How arguments are structured
points.brief: Writers order arguments to build, such as an anecdote first, then evidence, then a call to action.

points.title: Analysing visual material
points.brief: Images that go with an argument are analysed for how they support, sharpen or add to the written argument.

points.title: Argument in audio and video
points.brief: In audio and video, voice, sound, images and editing are used with the words to position an audience.

points.title: Context and the writer's identity
points.brief: Where a piece appears and who wrote it can change how an audience reacts to it.

points.title: Writing the argument analysis
points.brief: An analysis introduces the issue and texts, then follows the argument's structure, explaining how each part persuades.

points.title: Rebuttal and respectful disagreement
points.brief: Strong persuasive texts answer the other side's arguments and disagree with respect, keeping to the arguments rather than the person.

points.title: The spoken point of view
points.brief: Students present their own reasoned view on an issue aloud, using strong arguments, structure and techniques suited to the audience.
